Data Processing Overview：The dataset was imported from the orcas package and preprocessed by standardizing time fields, cleaning text entries, and separating multi-value fields (e.g., vessels, observers, pods) into individual rows. These steps enabled more granular and accurate analysis.

Question 1 : Temporal Pattern Analysis of Orca Encounters

1. Time frame of data collection

Code 
# Calculate the overall time span of the dataset
time_range <- orcas_tidy %>%
  summarise(
    start_date = min(date, na.rm = TRUE),
    end_date = max(date, na.rm = TRUE),
    total_days = as.numeric(end_date - start_date)
  )

time_range%>%
  kable(caption = "Time Range of Orca Dataset", 
        align = "l", format = "html") %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)%>%
  row_spec(0, bold = TRUE)
Time Range of Orca Dataset
start_date end_date total_days
2017-01-05 2024-10-06 2831

Data Overview:

The orca encounter dataset spans 8 years ( January 2017 to October 2024), providing 2831 days of comprehensive observation data.

2. Seasonal patterns by Month

Code 
# Observations by month to identify peak seasons
orcas_tidy %>%
  filter(!is.na(date)) %>%
  mutate(month = lubridate::month(date, label = TRUE, abbr = TRUE, locale = "C")) %>%
  count(month) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = month, y = n)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue2") +
  labs(title = "Monthly Distribution of Orca Observations", 
       subtitle = "from 2017-2024", 
       x = "Month", 
       y = "Number of Observations") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)+
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
    plot.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, face = "italic"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 12)
  )

Figure 1 reveals distinct seasonal patterns with peak encounter frequencies during summer and early fall months. September demonstrates the highest activity, followed by July and June. Winter months show significantly reduced activity, and this seasonal variation likely corresponds to orcas migration patterns.

3. Seasonal patterns by Year

Code 
# Analyze how monthly patterns vary across different years
orcas_tidy %>%
  filter(!is.na(date)) %>%
  mutate(
    year = year(date),
    month = month(date, label = TRUE, abbr = TRUE, locale = "C")
  ) %>%
  count(year, month) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = month, y = n, group = year, color = factor(year))) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 1.5) +
  labs(
    title = "Seasonal Patterns of Orca Observations by Year",
    subtitle = "Each line shows monthly observation counts per year (2017–2024)",
    x = "Month",
    y = "Number of Observations",
    color = "Year"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
    plot.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, face = "italic"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 12),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )

As shown in Figure 2, the core seasonal trend remains steady despite annual fluctuations. Observation levels were unusually high from June–September 2023 and noticeably lower during 2020–2021, which may reflect external influences, such as the COVID-19 pandemic.

4. Encounter duration analysis

Code 
enc_duration <- orcas_tidy %>%
  summarise(
    mean_duration = mean(duration_min, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_duration = median(duration_min, na.rm = TRUE)
    )

# Create violin plot
ggplot(orcas_tidy,aes(x = "", y = duration_min)) +
  geom_violin(fill = "lightblue", color = "steelblue2", alpha = 0.7, width = 0.6) +
  # Add the mean and median line
  geom_hline(yintercept = enc_duration$mean_duration, 
             color = "tomato2", 
             linewidth = 0.6, , 
             linetype = "dashed")+
  geom_hline(yintercept = enc_duration$median_duration, 
             color = "blue", 
             linewidth = 0.6,
             linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("text",
           x = 1,
           y = enc_duration$mean_duration,
           label = paste0("Mean: ", round(enc_duration$mean_duration,1), " min"),
           color = "tomato2",
           vjust = -0.5,
           size = 4) +
  annotate("text",
           x = 1,
           y = enc_duration$mean_duration,
           label = paste0("Median: ", round(enc_duration$median_duration,1), " min"),
           color = "blue",
           vjust = 2.5,
           size = 4) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Orca Encounter Duration",
    y = "Duration (mins)",
    x = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)+
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 12)
  )

Figure 3 shows the encounter durations average 124.6 (median: 100 minutes), indicating substantial observation periods suitable for detailed behavioral analysis. The right-skewed distribution shows that most encounters last 1-3 hours, with a few extending beyond 8 hours.

Question 2 : Spatial Pattern Analysis of Orca Encounters

1. Where are these encounters happening?

Code 
library(maps)

map_orcas_tidy <- orcas_tidy %>%
  filter(!is.na(begin_latitude), !is.na(begin_longitude),
         !is.na(end_latitude), !is.na(end_longitude)) 

# Get the latitude–longitude range
invisible(range(orcas_tidy$begin_latitude, na.rm = TRUE))
invisible(range(orcas_tidy$begin_longitude, na.rm = TRUE))

ggplot() +
    borders("world", colour = "black", fill = "grey80") +
    geom_point(data = map_orcas_tidy, 
               aes(x = begin_longitude, y = begin_latitude),
               color = "steelblue2", 
               alpha = 0.7, 
               size = 1) +
    coord_quickmap(xlim = c(-125.6, -122.4), 
                   ylim = c(48, 50)) +
    labs(
      title = "Orca Encounter Locations with Coastline",
      x = "Longitude",
      y = "Latitude"
    ) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12)+
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 12),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 10),
    panel.grid = element_line(color = "gray90")
  )

As shown in Figure 4, most orca encounters are primarily concentrated in the inland coastal waters between Vancouver Island and mainland British Columbia, particularly within the latitude range of 48°- 49.5°N and longitude range of 123°- 125°W. This area includes the southern Gulf Islands and San Juan Island, as shown in the map.

Most activity is clustered in protected inland waterways rather than the open Pacific Ocean, forming dense, consistent hotspots. These spatial patterns suggest relatively stable orca habitat preferences across years, especially within narrow channels and coastal zones.

2. Vessel movement patterns analysis

Code 
library(geosphere)

map_orcas_tidy <- orcas_tidy %>%
  filter(!is.na(begin_latitude), !is.na(begin_longitude),
         !is.na(end_latitude), !is.na(end_longitude)) %>%
  mutate(
    move_distance_km = distHaversine(
      p1 = cbind(begin_longitude, begin_latitude),
      p2 = cbind(end_longitude, end_latitude)
    ) / 1000)

# Calculate the average movement distance
mean_distance <- mean(map_orcas_tidy$move_distance_km, na.rm = TRUE)

# Create density plot
ggplot(map_orcas_tidy, aes(x = move_distance_km)) +
  geom_density(fill = "lightblue", 
               color = "steelblue", 
               alpha = 0.6, 
               linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean_distance, 
             linetype = "dashed", 
             color = "tomato", 
             linewidth = 1) +
  annotate("text",
           x = mean_distance, 
           y = 0.01,
           label = paste0("Mean: ", round(mean_distance, 1), " km"),
           hjust = -0.1, 
           color = "tomato", 
           size = 4,
           fontface = "bold") +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Vessel Movement Distances",
       x = "Movement Distance (km)", 
       y = "Density") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 12),
    panel.grid.minor.x = element_line(color = "grey90"),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank()
  )
Code 
library(sf)

# Extract the top 5 vessels
top_vessel_track <- map_orcas_tidy %>%
  filter(!is.na(vessel)) %>%
  count(vessel, sort = TRUE) %>%
  slice_max(n, n = 5) %>% 
  pull(vessel)

# Create vessel track map
map_orcas_tidy %>% 
  filter(vessel %in% top_vessel_track) %>% 
  ggplot() +
  borders("world", colour = "black", fill = "grey80") +
  geom_segment(aes(x = begin_longitude, y = begin_latitude,
                   xend = end_longitude, yend = end_latitude,
                   color = vessel),
               arrow = arrow(type = "closed", length = unit(0.1, "cm")),
               linewidth = 0.5, alpha = 0.7) +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(-125, -122.4), 
                 ylim = c(48, 49.5))+
  labs(
    title = "Encounter Tracks by Vessel",
    subtitle = "Arrows showing direction from encounter start to end",
    x = "Longitude",
    y = "Latitude",
    color = "Vessel"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.title.align = 0.5,
    aspect.ratio = 0.8,
    plot.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, face = "italic"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 12),
  )+
  scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0))

Because the full set of vessel tracks is visually cluttered, we refined the visualization by filtering to the top 5 most active vessels.

Based on the Figure 5 and Figure 6 , the analysis shows that vessel movements pattern during encounters are mostly short and localized, with an average movement distance of 10.3 km. This suggests vessels either find whales quickly or operate in small, concentrated areas.

The tracks reveal clear directional patterns with arrows indicating movement from the start to the end points of each encounter. Different vessels like Kcb III, Mike 1, and Orcinus showing distinct tracking behaviors, that some follow tight, clustered, localized paths near whale pods, often moving in relatively short, linear routes.

Repeated use of similar paths indicates routine patrolling or predictable whale locations in these areas.

Question 3 : Analysis of Encounters by Vessels and Observers

Code 
# Clean and standardizing the pod column
orcas_tidy <- orcas_tidy %>%
  mutate(
    pods_or_ecotype = str_replace_all(pods_or_ecotype, "(?i)\\s+[Aa]nd\\s+", ","),
    pods_or_ecotype = str_replace_all(pods_or_ecotype, "/", ","),
    pods_or_ecotype = str_replace_all(pods_or_ecotype, "&", ","),
    pods_or_ecotype = str_replace_all(pods_or_ecotype, "\\s*\\([^\\)]+\\)", ""),  
    pods_or_ecotype = case_when(
      str_detect(pods_or_ecotype, 
                 regex("Bigg.?s.*killer.*whales", 
                       ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "Bigg's killer whales",
      str_detect(pods_or_ecotype, 
                 regex("Bigg's$", 
                       ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "Bigg's killer whales",
      str_detect(pods_or_ecotype, 
                 regex("Transient", 
                       ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "Bigg's killer whales",
      TRUE ~ pods_or_ecotype
    ),
    pods_or_ecotype = str_replace_all(pods_or_ecotype, "(?i)\\s*pods?\\s*", ""),
    pods_or_ecotype = if_else(
      str_detect(pods_or_ecotype, 
                 regex("^Bigg's(\\s|$)", 
                       ignore_case = TRUE)),
      pods_or_ecotype, 
      str_replace_all(pods_or_ecotype, "'[sS]", ",")
    ),
    pods_or_ecotype = str_replace(pods_or_ecotype, "^(?i)And\\s+", ""),
    pods_or_ecotype = str_squish(pods_or_ecotype),
    pods_or_ecotype = str_squish(pods_or_ecotype),
  )%>%
  separate_rows(pods_or_ecotype, sep = ",") %>%
  mutate(pods_or_ecotype = str_trim(pods_or_ecotype)) %>%
  filter(pods_or_ecotype != "")

1. Which Orca Pods Are Seen the Most Often?

Code 
# Identify which pods are encountered most often
top_pod <- orcas_tidy %>%
  count(pods_or_ecotype, sort = TRUE) %>%
  slice_max(n, n = 10, with_ties = FALSE) 

top_pod %>%
  rename(`Pod / Ecotype` = pods_or_ecotype,
         `Encounters` = n) %>%
  kable(caption = "Top 10 Frequently Observed Orcas", 
        align = "l", format = "html") %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)%>%
  row_spec(0, bold = TRUE)
Code 
# Calculate the encounters of top pods by year 
top_pod_yearly <- orcas_tidy %>%
filter(pods_or_ecotype %in% top_pod$pods_or_ecotype, !is.na(date)) %>%
mutate(year = lubridate::year(date),
       pods_or_ecotype = factor(pods_or_ecotype, 
                                levels = top_pod$pods_or_ecotype)
) %>%
count(year, pods_or_ecotype)

# Plot line chart to display annual trend
ggplot(top_pod_yearly, aes(x = year, y = n, color = pods_or_ecotype)) +
geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
geom_point() +
labs(
title = "Yearly Encounter Trends for Top 10 Orca Pods",
subtitle = "From 2017 to 2024",
x = "Year",
y = "Number of Encounters",
color = "Pod"
) +
theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
theme(
  plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
  plot.subtitle = element_text(face = "italic", size = 11),
  legend.position = "bottom",
  legend.title = element_text(size = 11),
  legend.text = element_text(size = 10)
  )

From Table 1 we can know Bigg’s killer whales were the most frequently observed ecotype, followed by Southern Resident groups include J, L and K pods. Same whale groups consistently appear across multiple years

As shown in Figure 7, Bigg’s killer whales were the most frequently encountered group across all years, with a clear upward trend since 2017. Among the Southern Resident killer whales, the J, K, and L pods were consistently observed, though at lower and more variable frequencies. These repeated appearances suggest that certain pods are reliably present in the region year after year, reflecting stable movement patterns or preferred habitats.

2. Most active vessels and observers in Orca Encounters

Code 
# Count total encounters per vessel
top_vessel <- orcas_tidy %>%
  filter(!is.na(vessel)) %>%
  count(vessel, sort = TRUE) %>%
  slice_max(n, n = 10)%>%
  mutate(
    share = n / sum(n),
    label = paste0(vessel, "\n", round(share * 100), "%")
  )%>%
  arrange(desc(share)) %>%
  mutate(vessel = factor(vessel, levels = unique(vessel)),
         label = ifelse(share > 0.05, 
                        scales::percent(share, accuracy = 1), ""))

# Create pie chart
ggplot(top_vessel, aes(x = "", y = share, fill = vessel)) +
  geom_col(width = 1, color = "white") +
  coord_polar(theta = "y") +
  geom_text(aes(label = label),
            position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5),
            size = 5, color = "black") +
  labs(title = "% of Orca Encounters by Top 10 Active Vessels") +
  theme_void(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "right",
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14))

As shown in Figure 8, the vessels Orcinus and Mike 1 stand out as the most active vessels, collectively accounting for nearly 80% of all orca encounters. Their frequent involvement shows their pivotal role in data collection and long-term monitoring efforts.

Code 
# Count encounters by observer 
top_observer <- orcas_tidy %>%
  filter(!is.na(observers)) %>%
  count(observers, sort = TRUE) %>%
  slice_max(n, n = 10)  %>%
  mutate(
    share = n / sum(n),
    label = ifelse(share > 0.05, 
                   scales::percent(share, accuracy = 1), ""),
    observers = factor(observers, levels = observers[order(-share)]))

# Create pie chart
ggplot(top_observer, aes(x = "", y = share, fill = observers)) +
  geom_col(width = 1, color = "white") +
  coord_polar(theta = "y") +
  geom_text(aes(label = label),
            position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5),
            size = 5, color = "black") +
  labs(title = "% of Encounters by Top 10 Active Observers") +
  theme_void(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "right",
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14))

As shown in Figure 9, more than half of all documented orca encounters were contributed by a small core of dedicated and highly active observers, especially Dave Ellifrit and Mark Malleson. This reflects strong continuity and expertise in long-term data collection.

3. Vessel-Pod relationship analysis

Code 
# Analyze which vessels encounter which pod types most frequently
vessel_pod_encounters <- orcas_tidy %>%
  filter(vessel %in% top_vessel$vessel,
         pods_or_ecotype %in% top_pod$pods_or_ecotype) %>%
  count(vessel, pods_or_ecotype, name = "encounters")

# Plot heatmap showing vessel-pod encounter patterns
ggplot(vessel_pod_encounters, aes(x = pods_or_ecotype, 
                           y = reorder(vessel, encounters), 
                           fill = encounters)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "lightblue", high = "darkblue") +
  labs(
    title = "Top 10 Vessels and Their Pod Encounters",
    x = "Orca Ecotype",
    y = "Vessel",
    fill = "Number of Encounters"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    legend.title = element_text(size = 11),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 10))

As shown in Figure 10, the most active vessels, especially Orcinus and Mike 1, encountered a wide range of orca pods. Orcinus had high encounters with all major groups, showing its broad research focus. Mike 1 also had frequent encounters, especially with Bigg’s and J,K,L pods, suggesting a focus on certain ecotypes. Other vessels like Kcb III and Morning Star had fewer total encounters but were more focused on specific pods.

Overall, the data shows a clear pattern that some vessels specialize in certain pods, while others provide broad coverage, helping build the record of orca populations.

5. Average Encounter Duration per Vessel

Code 
vessel_mean_dur <- enc_duration$mean_duration

# Calculate the stats of vessel encounter duration
vessel_duration <- orcas_tidy %>%
  filter(!is.na(vessel), !is.na(duration_min)) %>%
  group_by(vessel) %>%
  summarise(mean_duration = mean(duration_min, na.rm = TRUE),
            max_duration = max(duration_min, na.rm = TRUE),
            long_encounters  = sum(duration_min > vessel_mean_dur, na.rm = TRUE),
            num_encounters = n(),
            .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  # Only vessels with 5+ encounters
  filter(num_encounters >= 5) %>% 
  arrange(desc(mean_duration))
  
# Create the bar chart
ggplot(vessel_duration, aes(x = reorder(vessel, -mean_duration),
                            y = mean_duration)) +
  geom_col(fill = "coral2") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = vessel_mean_dur, 
             linetype = "dashed", 
             linewidth = 1, 
             color = "blue4") +
  annotate("text", x = 1, y = vessel_mean_dur + 30, 
           label = paste0("Overall avgerage mins: ", 
                          round(vessel_mean_dur, 1), " mins"), 
           hjust = 0, size = 4, color = "blue4") +
  labs(
    title = "Average Encounter Duration by Vessel",
    x = "Vessel",
    y = "Mean Duration (mins)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
    plot.title = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 12))

Some vessel names, such as Orcinus Chimo remain partially merged due to data cleaning limits, but this does not impact the overall analysis.

Based on the analysis shown in Figure 12, Orcinus had the longest average encounter time, well above the overall average duration. Other vessels, like Initial Observation and Springtime, also had extended observation times, suggesting detailed research work.

In contrast, high-activity vessels like Mike 1 and Kcb III had shorter average durations, indicating more frequent but quicker encounters.

This suggests that different vessels employ different research styles, with some focusing on in-depth encounters and others prioritizing broad coverage.

Question 4 : Common Words analysis

Code 
library(tidytext)
library(stopwords)
data("stop_words") 

# Word Tokenize
orcas_words <- orcas_tidy %>%
  select(encounter_summary) %>%
  filter(!is.na(encounter_summary))%>%
  unnest_tokens(word, encounter_summary)%>%
  filter(!word %in% stop_words$word,
         !word %in% c("whale", "whales", "orca", "orcas", "pod", "pods", "encounter"))
         
# Top 20 Words
top_words <- orcas_words %>% 
  count(word, sort = TRUE) %>% 
  slice_max(n, n = 20) %>%
  rename(count = n)
  
top_words%>%
  kable(caption = "Top 20 common words", 
        align = "l", format = "html") %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)%>%

Word Filtering Explanation :

Common stop words and general terms like “whale”, “orca”, “pod”, and “encounter” were removed before analysis. These words appear in almost every summary and do not add useful information. This step helps highlight more specific and meaningful content in the encounter descriptions.

Summaries of Common Words :

  • The most common words in the encounter summaries include location related terms like “south”, “north”, “island”, and “west”. These words show that observers often describe where the orcas were seen and the direction they were moving.
  • Action words such as “headed”, “heading”, and “left” are also frequent. This suggests that many summaries include details about orcas movement.
  • Some words, like “team” and “mark”, may refer to people involved in the observations. These are less useful for understanding orcas behavior.
  • Depending on the research goal, it may be helpful to remove location names and people’s names to focus more on behavior-related words.
